11249-four-famous-american-writers-washi:
Sherwin Cody's 1899 book for young Americans profiles four writers: Washington Irving, Edgar Allan Poe, James Russell Lowell, and Bayard Taylor. Irving's chapters follow him from childhood up the Hudson to Rip Van Winkle and the Alhambra; Poe's trace his artistry, college years. The writing of The Raven; Lowell's cover Elmwood, law, and the Biglow papers; Taylor's recount a penniless European tramp tour and a career as traveler-poet.

Cody writes biography as encouragement, showing each writer learning his craft through effort and setback. The book's schoolroom tone now reads as period evidence about which authors adults wanted children to admire. It still serves as a friendly first introduction to four very different American careers.
13002-what-i-saw-in-california-a-descrip:
Edwin Bryant, late alcalde of San Francisco, published What I Saw in California in 1849 as a guide for intending emigrants. It describes soil, climate, productions, and gold mines, with the best routes, a map, and an appendix of official documents and assayed gold values. Bryant quotes Dryden: all which I saw, and part of which I was.

A mountain passage shows the journey. Bear and venison hang for winter, a giant named Turner swears beyond all former examples, and a rainy return passes Barnett's empty house with an Indian pilot left at his rancheria. Bryant writes as pioneer and promoter. The book is a key gold-rush source.
13009-the-reign-of-andrew-jackson-a-chro:
Frederic Austin Ogg's 1919 volume, number twenty in the Chronicles of America series, traces Andrew Jackson from frontier fighter to president. Ogg follows Jackson through the Creek War, the victory at New Orleans, the taking of Florida, and the fall of the old caucus system. Later chapters take up the Webster-Hayne debate, tariff and nullification, the war on the Bank, and the removal of southern Indians.

The narrative stresses how frontier politics reshaped the nation, turning a general into a symbol of popular rule. Ogg also notes Jackson's unhappy months as governor of Florida, where vague powers and a lack of patronage left him thwarted. Written for general readers, the book offers a compact, readable life of a presidency that still divides opinion.
1317-saltbush-bill-j-p:
A. B. Paterson, the Australian poet of "Waltzing Matilda," gathers bush ballads around Saltbush Bill, a drover and justice of the peace, and his mates. The poems tell of droving, shearing, and the law of the outback, in rollicking verse full of horses, dust, and humor.

Paterson writes the bush with a horseman's eye and a storyteller's verve. The ballads are meant to be read aloud. The book suits readers who like Australian verse at its most lively and true. Paterson's ballads are meant to be read aloud, with verve.
15836-expositions-of-holy-scripture-ezek:
A volume of sermons by Alexander MacLaren, the Scottish Baptist preacher, issued by George H. Doran Company in New York. MacLaren, famed for clear, warm exposition, takes Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Minor Prophets, then Matthew chapters one to eight. Each sermon treats one passage with care and plain speech. The book served preachers and Bible readers alike.

Ezekiel sermons include chambers of imagery, the holy nation, dry bones and the spirit of life, and the river of life. Daniel brings youthful confessors, the image and the stone, and harmless fires. Minor prophets and early Matthew follow in the same steady manner. The volume still helps readers who want scripture opened slowly, passage by passage, with heart as well as mind.
16378-the-art-of-perfumery-and-methods-o:
The Art of Perfumery and Method of Obtaining the Odors of Plants teaches readers to make perfumes from garden and field. Its opening pages describe the drying house, where herbs hang in bunches from the rafters and rose leaves dry in warm cupboards heated by a flue from a fire below. Flower buds rest on canvas trays twelve feet long by four feet wide, shelved until dry.

Later instructions cover perfumes for the handkerchief, scented powders, odorous vinegars, dentifrices, pomatums, cosmetiques, and perfumed soap. The book joins gardening, chemistry, and craft in a practical Victorian voice. Readers curious about scent making will find a fragrant, detailed manual.
17021-watch-and-clock-escapements-a-comp:
This 1904 Keystone manual gives a full study of watch and clock escapements, the small parts that meter time. Chapters cover the detached lever, the cylinder, and the chronometer escapements, plus a history of the escapement and a guide to fitting a new cylinder. Nearly two hundred original pictures show each part and step.

Compiled from Keystone serials, the book speaks to makers and repairers in plain, exact terms. It skips long history in the main chapters to give full plans for drawing and building each type. Clock fans and horology students will find a classic workshop text, still clear on how a good watch keeps true time.
18094-history-of-the-girondists-volume-i:
Alphonse de Lamartine wrote the History of the Girondists, or Personal Memoirs of the Patriots of the French Revolution, from unpublished sources, translated by H. T. Ryde. Volume one was printed in London in 1856 by Henry G. Bohn.

Book one opens with Mirabeau, his marriage, his entry to the Assembly, his master mind, and his death, then turns to Rousseau, Voltaire, Louis XVI, and the clubs. Robespierre, Lafayette, and the rival champions fill the later pages. Lamartine writes with a poet's warmth and a patriot's eye. It is a vivid, romantic history of the Revolution's first years.
18261-operation-r-s-v-p:
Writing as H. Beam Piper, the author of this short story told it through a set of formal diplomatic letters dated in 1984. The letters pass between ministers of two rival powers, one based in Eastern Europe and one in East Asia. Their polite wording hides sharp threats, and the main subject is a new nuclear rocket missile called Marxist Victory.

Each letter answers the last, and the exchange turns on a test firing, a disputed river, and a feared blast at a secret uranium plant at Khatanga. The humor comes from the gap between courtly manners and open menace. Readers get a compact Cold War satire in which world danger arrives by post, one stiff note at a time.
18862-the-uncollected-writings-of-thomas:
James Hogg edited this first volume of Thomas De Quincey's uncollected writings for Swan Sonnenschein of London in 1890. Hogg had known De Quincey closely from 1850 until the author's death in 1859, helping him prepare his Selections Grave and Gay for the press.

The volume gathers essays and stories left out of the collected works, with notes on the circumstances of each piece and the evidence for De Quincey's authorship. Hogg believed his friend would have set several of them beside Suspiria de Profundis, which he calls the highest reach of De Quincey's impassioned power. The book offers readers the last fruit off an old tree, in Landor's phrase, and a fuller view of a great essayist.
18871-a-channel-passage-and-other-poems-:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's volume six of his collected poems gathers A Midsummer Holiday, Astrophel, and A Channel Passage and Other Poems. The volume lists his earlier collections alongside, from Poems and Ballads through Tristram of Lyonesse and Atalanta in Calydon. This selection presents his later verse in the collected edition's order.

Readers will find Swinburne's musical, richly rhymed lyricism applied to holidays, the sea, and elegy, with his usual command of meter and sound. The Channel passage of the title gives the book its sea air. Readers get a solid sample of late Swinburne, best read aloud, and a useful way into a poet whose reputation rests on sound as much as sense.
19009-sir-joshua-reynolds-a-collection-o:
Estelle M. Hurll prepared this volume on Sir Joshua Reynolds for the Masterpieces of Art series, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1900. It presents fifteen pictures by Reynolds, with a portrait of the painter by himself as frontispiece, and adds an introduction and interpretation by Hurll. A historical directory and a table of his life's principal events support the plates.

Among the pictures are Penelope Boothby and Master Crewe as Henry VIII, with notes on each work and its place in Reynolds's career. Hurll explains composition, feeling, and technique for general readers. Readers get an accessible art book from the age of carbon prints, useful for meeting Reynolds's portraits without visiting a gallery.
19229-anticipations-of-the-reaction-of-m:
H. G. Wells wrote this 1902 second edition, Anticipations of the Reaction of Mechanical and Scientific Progress upon Human Life and Thought. Chapters forecast locomotion, great cities, social elements, democracy, war, languages, and faith in the twentieth century. Wells argues from trends, not prophecy alone.

He imagines a road system where new vehicles join traffic at once, letting travellers run seventy miles an hour without change, against railways frozen by old patterns. Short-sighted progress, he warns, ends in a cul-de-sac. Readers get a bold Edwardian forecast, brilliant, speculative, and often prescient.
19606-illustrated-catalogue-of-the-colle:
James Stevenson prepared this illustrated catalogue of collections from the Pueblos of Zuni, New Mexico, and Walpi, Arizona, gathered in eighteen eighty-one for the Bureau of Ethnology. Stone axes, metates, and mortars open the Zuni list, followed by clay water jars, pitchers, bowls, and cooking pots.

Basketry, loom tools, dance gear, gambling tools, and items of horn, bone, feather, and skin fill later pages, with a shorter Walpi section to close. The catalogue remains a detailed record of Pueblo craft at a moment of rapid change. The Zuni pottery entries sort eating bowls by yellow, red, and decorated ware, each with its own catalog number.
2009-the-origin-of-species-by-means-of-n:
Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, argues that species change over time through natural selection, the survival of those best fitted to their surroundings. Darwin builds the case from pigeons, barnacles, and the finches of the Galápagos, and from the breeding of domestic animals.

The book's argument, published in 1859, changed biology and much else besides, and its prose is careful, modest, and full of observed fact. Readers approaching it for the first time will find a work of science that reads like a long, patient letter. That still rewards reading whole rather than in quotation.
20090-the-uncollected-writings-of-thomas:
Thomas De Quincey, famed for his opium tale, left much work uncollected in his lifetime. Volume two of his uncollected writings gathers later essays, with notes by James Hogg. Three pieces deal with Chinese affairs from a tense time. War with China then seemed close, the notes explain in detail.

Those pieces first ran in Titan in February and April 1857. They then came out as a scarce pamphlet of 152 pages. Hogg adds a long preface and clear notes for new readers. The volume suits readers who want De Quincey beyond his best-known book.
21057-the-log-of-the-flying-fish-a-story:
Harry Collingwood's novel of aerial and submarine peril is often counted among the early works of science fiction. A German professor living in London recruits rich, adventurous Englishmen for a bold voyage. Their craft, the Flying Fish, is built from a new material called aetherium.

Because aetherium is both very light and very strong, the vessel can rise into the air and dive deep under the sea. The crew reach the North Pole, find the remains of a Viking ship, and visit Africa and Mount Everest. Young readers of the time got invention, travel, and danger in one tale.
22060-the-young-franc-tireurs-and-their-:
G. A. Henty wrote The Young Franc-Tireurs for boys who liked their history with gunpowder. The story opens as the Franco-Prussian War breaks out in 1870. Henty had seen the franc-tireurs, France's volunteer irregulars, during the war itself. He judged them brave but too often badly led, and his preface says so plainly.

Two young heroes join the irregulars and march for the Vosges. They fight at the tunnel of Saverne, hunt a traitor, and face desperate odds. Henty packs the tale with real places and events from the war. For Victorian schoolboys, such books were history lessons that read like adventure, and Henty was their master.
22484-gardening-indoors-and-under-glass-:
F. F. Rockwell wrote Gardening Indoors and Under Glass in 1911. It is a practical guide to the propagation and care of house plants. Coldframes and the small greenhouse fall under its title's promise.

Rockwell begins with light, the first need of indoor plants. Almost all plants need an abundance of light, flowering or not. Many require sunshine, especially during dull winter days. Without it, stems grow long, lanky, and weak, he warns. Foliage takes a washed-out, semi-transparent look in poor light. Such plants fall easy victims to disease or insect enemies. His plain rules still serve winter gardeners. The book preserves expert house-plant care from before modern grow lights.
24907-the-lady-and-the-pirate-being-the-:
Emerson Hough published The Lady and the Pirate in Indianapolis in 1913, with pictures by Harry A. Mathes. The narrator calls himself a caitiff, then a captive, then a pirate, and sails for the Spanish Main with a fair captive at his side. Chapters run from parley and capture to treasure, boarding actions, and hue and cry.

Helena, the captive maiden, spars with her captor in bright talk, even as she plots escape and he plots love. Hough writes with humor and high color, in the style of his Mississippi Bubble. Readers who like pirate romances with wit will enjoy a tale where the pirate's worst foe is his own heart.
25491-peck-s-sunshine-being-a-collection:
George W. Peck collects short pieces first written for Peck's Sun in Milwaukee into this 1882 volume, promising sunshine in place of clouds for its readers. He opens with a mock courtroom plea, joking that he stands charged with trying to remove the people of America by publishing a new book.

The articles that follow mix jokes, satire, and plain talk about daily life, politics, and human folly, all in the brisk newspaper voice that made the Sun popular. Read together, they show Peck's method: a quick setup, a comic twist, and a moral nudge delivered without preaching.
28921-an-essay-on-true-and-apparent-beau:
Pierre Nicole wrote this essay on true and apparent beauty, translated by J. V. Cunningham for the Augustan Reprint Society in 1950. The full title promises grounds, from settled principles, for choosing and rejecting epigrams. The Clark Memorial Library at the University of California published it as number twenty-four, with general editors from Michigan, Yale, Columbia, and Chicago.

Nicole, a French moralist of the classical age, argues about taste and judgment in short poems, separating real beauty from show. Cunningham's translation makes a rare text available to English readers. Scholars of French literature and of epigram get a compact, principled essay, with notes tracing its sources in the Greek anthology in France and Italy.
28959-the-illustrated-works-of-gordon-ho:
David Widger edited this linked index to the illustrated works of Gordon Home, author and painter, who lived from 1878 to 1969. The index covers Normandy, Yorkshire, Yorkshire Coast and Moorlands, England of My Heart, Beautiful Britain, and The Evolution of an English Town. The Normandy chapters run from the banks of the Seine and Rouen to Lisieux, Falaise, Mont St. Michel, and Caen.

Home's colored and line pictures stand beside his text, showing Mont St. Michel from the causeway, Chateau Gaillard above the Seine, and the church at Gisors. The index lists every picture and chapter, so a reader can tour a county through Home's eyes. It serves as a guide to a popular English travel writer and artist, whose books taught readers to look at their own countryside.
31249-conspecificity-of-two-pocket-mice-:
E. Raymond Hall and Marilyn Bailey Ogilvie's 1960 paper argues that two named pocket mice are one species. Perognathus goldmani and Perognathus artus, from southern Sonora, northern Sinaloa, and adjoining Chihuahua and Durango, belong to the intermedius group and the subgenus Chaetodipus. Until now the literature treated them as two species.

Both share buff upper parts strongly mixed with black, a buff lateral line, and white underparts, though goldmani runs larger with more inflated ear bullae. A transect across southeastern Sonora shows intergradation from the largest animals at the Río Yaqui Reservoir to the smallest southeast of Alamos, and the authors conclude the two are conspecific.
31412-old-and-new-london-volume-i-a-narr:
Volume one of Old and New London offers a large illustrated narrative of the city's history, its people, and its places. Plates show the Thames Embankment, the Royal Exchange and Bank of England, St. Paul's from Ludgate Circus, a Holborn viaduct, and a city apprentice of the sixteenth century, among many other scenes. The text moves district by district, pairing history with the streets and buildings a reader could still walk.

The volume's scale is its point: London is treated as a living record, where each quarter carries its own past. Readers interested in the city will find anecdote, topography, and social history woven together. Even where later research has corrected details, the book remains a rich Victorian portrait of London old and new.
33620-a-flight-in-spring-in-the-car-luca:
The Reverend J. Harris Knowles recounts a private railway journey in the car Lucania from New York to the Pacific coast and back during April and May 1898. Seven hundred and fifty copies were privately printed for Frederick Humphreys. Knowles dedicates his random jottings to his fellow travelers, nicknamed the King and Queen, the Apostle and the Angel, the Fairy Princess, Juno and Psyche, and the Spanish Count.

The narrative moves from the start and the car's kitchen, cook, poetic dinner, and improvised theatricals through Philadelphia, Washington, Thomasville, Montgomery, and New Orleans, with war declared along the way. Southern flowers, old plantations, Jackson Square, cathedrals, cemeteries, and the French Market fill the pages. The book is a charming, first-hand record of luxury rail travel at the moment America went to war with Spain.
33671-mary-the-help-of-christians-novena:
The Reverend Bonaventure Hammer compiled this volume of novenas in preparation for the principal (main) feasts of the Blessed Virgin. Rules for the proper observance of novenas and guidance on reading meditations and observing practices open the book, followed by an introduction to Mary, Help of Christians.

Novenas (nine-day prayers) honor the Immaculate Conception, the Nativity, and further feasts, each with nine days of meditation. These include predestination (God's choice from the start), immaculate conception, victory over Satan, freedom from actual sin, fullness of grace, refuge, mother of chastity, and the feast itself, among others. The volume gives Catholic readers a structured, traditional devotion for the Marian year, in the clear, practical style of Hammer's other compilations.
3643-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Albert Bigelow Paine's writings on Mark Twain, the eleventh in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Paine, Twain's official biographer, knew the humorist in his last years and wrote at length about his life, work, and talk. This file lifts short passages from Paine's writings for browsing.

Readers meet Twain through his biographer's eyes: anecdotes, judgments, and remembered sayings in brief form. The set works as a companion to Paine's full biography and to Twain's own books. It suits readers who want a quick taste of Twain's world, as seen by the man who lived and worked beside him.
4350-physics-and-politics-or-thoughts-on:
Walter Bagehot wrote this book to apply the ideas of natural selection and inheritance to political society. His contents run from the preliminary age and the use of conflict through nation-making to the age of discussion and verifiable progress. The first chapter notes the sudden growth of physical knowledge in his own lifetime.

Railways and telegraphs, Bagehot writes, have made a new world around readers in fifty years. He asks how societies, like species, form habits, harden into nations, and then learn to argue and change. The book is a classic of Victorian social thought, compact, witty, and still quoted on custom, imitation, and the conditions of free government.
6185-a-romany-of-the-snows-complete-bein:
Parker's complete Romany of the Snows gathers five volumes continuing Pierre and His People and the last records of Pretty Pierre. Volume one crosses jumping sandhills with a lovely bully, a filibuster, and a simple king's gift, while volume two gives Malachi and the Lake of the Great Slave.

Later volumes add the Bridge House, epaulettes, Little Babiche, sun dogs, and the cruise of the Ninety-Nine. Parker inscribes the tales to Sir William Van Horne, noting some stories were begotten in late gossip by his fireside. This complete edition is described from its contents and dedication, covering the whole cycle.
7928-the-poet-s-poet-essays-on-the-chara:
Elizabeth Atkins, an instructor in English at the University of Minnesota, wrote these essays on what poets themselves have said about their own calling. Her span is English verse of the last hundred and fifty years, and she argues that a poet's self-judgment deserves more attention than critics usually give it. She tests that claim against Plato's old challenge to poetry as well as against the poets' own words.

The chapters gather statements by poets about their character and mission, reading them as evidence about how poetry works. Students of literature get a guided tour of verse as self-portrait, not just as finished art. The book remains useful for anyone asking why poets write, what they think they are for, and how they defend their art against its critics.
8860-palestine-or-the-holy-land-from-the:
Michael Russell, clergyman and scholar, writes Palestine, or the Holy Land, from the earliest period to the present time, with a map as frontispiece. His preface faces the author's choice: simple history on one hand, or mere local description on the other, with the book's character determined by which is chosen. Earlier volumes on Palestine, he notes, give either a bare abridgment of Jewish annals or a topographical delineation of country, cities, and towns.

Russell tries to join both, narrating the land's history while describing its places, peoples, and antiquities. The result is a solid early nineteenth-century survey, informed by travel accounts and biblical scholarship of its day. Readers interested in the Holy Land's history, or in how Europeans pictured it before modern archaeology, will find a thorough, readable introduction, best supplemented now by newer work.
9185-the-mystery-of-murray-davenport-a-s:
Robert Neilson Stephens wrote this New York mystery in 1903, in the city of his own day. Its narrator, Mr. Larcher, goes out in the rain, out of suits with fortune, and meets a ready-money man, a lodging by the river, and a name, Turl, that keeps surfacing. Florence declares her allegiance as the plot thickens.

Larcher puts this and that together, corners Turl, and hears a strange design unfold. Stephens keeps the pace brisk and the streets vivid. The novel is a neat sample of the urban mystery tale just before the age of the hard-boiled detective.
a-channel-passage-and-other-poems-taken-: Algernon Charles Swinburne gathers poems from the sixth volume of his collected works. The title poem, A Channel Passage, stands beside other poems and tales from his later verse. The volume also recalls A Midsummer Holiday and Astrophel from the same collection. Swinburne's music and imagery run through sea pieces, meditations, and songs.
a-romany-of-the-snows-complete-being-a-c:
A Romany of the Snows, complete, by Gilbert Parker, gathers all five volumes of the last records of Pretty Pierre in one text. Parker presents Pierre, the French Canadian wanderer of Pierre and His People, as narrator and witness across the whole Canadian North. The contents run from Across the Jumping Sandhills and A Lovely Bully in the first volume to the sea going Cruise of the Ninety-Nine at the end.

Between those poles stand Malachi's hanging, the Red Patrol, the Bridge House on the Madawaska, Little Babiche's Christmas testimony, and the trail of the sun dogs. Fur governors, mounted police, river drivers, smugglers, and priests people a North where law is distant and character is fate. Read whole, the set is Parker's epic of the Dominion's wild decades, told by the one man who walked out of every story in it and remembered them all.
anticipations-of-the-reaction-of-mechani: Herbert George Wells writes Anticipations of the reaction of mechanical and scientific progress upon human life and thought. The book forecasts how railways, motors, and new weapons will reshape cities, war, and society. Wells's bold guesses made the work a landmark of futurology, argued with energy and confidence. Some guesses hit home, and some miss wide.
doe-osti-17019152-doe-level-2-milestone-:
Milestone report from Lawrence Livermore, dated September 2026, records a performance test campaign on the National Ignition Facility laser. Gordon Brunton, Jean-Michel Di Nicola, Sam Schrauth, and a large team report on work tied to Enhanced Yield Capability. The test point named in the title is 2.6 megajoules at 450 terawatts, full facility scale.

One bundle of eight beamlines was upgraded with two added amplifier slabs in each line, plus flashlamp, shielding, and control changes. That bundle passed its energy aims with margin to spare. A later four beamline quad then delivered about 54.2 kilojoules of ultraviolet energy, matching the full scale test point, across four reliable shots.
doe-osti-17073818-sample-to-hazard-asses:
Tom Bates of Lawrence Livermore led SHARP, a risk based platform for judging unknown biological samples, reported in October 2026. Threats from outbreaks, accidents, or misuse can involve organisms on no watch list, and naming an organism does not show what it does. The platform moves from a raw sample toward a hazard judgment in linked steps.

Sample preparation and enrichment improved pathogen detection by up to one thousand fold under the tested conditions. A broad screen ran on clinical nasal swab samples, and software recovered expected toxin related test sequences from control samples. Structure based tools then predicted which candidates would act in the body, lab methods tested peptide activity on human nerve proteins, and a final pipeline forecast adverse health effects.
doe-osti-17076591-lucid-epidemiologic-da:
Hilda Klasky, John Gounley, and Heidi Hanson of Oak Ridge document version 18.5 of the LUCID pipeline in September 2026. LUCID cleans up occupational health data sets so studies can be combined. Public radiation worker data sets hold rich records, but each study used its own names, codes, date formats, exposure units, and missing value habits.

The pipeline aligns those differences automatically and runs model based quality checks on the result. Harmonized data can then feed cross cohort analysis, AI workflows, and risk modeling on a shared footing. Appendices carry developer and user documentation for the release, so other teams can run and extend the same pipeline.
doe-osti-2564609-an-investigation-of-cri:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-24329, issued March 24, 2026, asks how deep corrosion pits can get before a storage container fails its drop test. Tristan Karns, Jonathan Gigax, Gabriel Longoria, and five co-authors studied the SAVY-4000, a container used for nuclear material storage. Pitting corrosion is a known weakness of these containers, and pits could matter in an accident drop.

Six five-quart containers were exposed to 6.0 molar hydrochloric acid gas for 152 to 159 days, until all showed pitting. Each test package, weighing at least 18.1 kilograms, was then dropped from 3.66 meters, the top working height in the safety rules. After the drops, the team measured the damage and re-examined the pits. Pits sitting in the dented region had not cracked, at least for the pit sizes this exposure produced.
doe-osti-2572570-vitrification-testing-o:
Report HFO-72188, also numbered VSL-19R4490-1, from the Vitreous State Laboratory of the Catholic University of America, was published in June 2025. Keith S. Matlack, Wing K. Kot, Hao Gan, and Ian L. Pegg wrote it for the Department of Energy's Office of River Protection, with Innocent Joseph of Atkins Energy. The tests ask how high-level waste rich in phosphate behaves when it is vitrified, melted into glass for disposal.

Work ran on the DM100 melter system, a small test melter with its own feed and off-gas trains. Sections lay out the test objectives, quality assurance, and experimental methods before turning to results. Phosphate-heavy waste is a known headache for glass formulation, since phosphate can separate out of the melt. The report documents how the chosen feeds and glasses performed across the melter runs, giving the river protection program data for full-scale design decisions.
doe-osti-2584242-status-and-trends-in-th:
Annual market report NREL/TP-6A20-92289 counts America's voluntary green power market for 2023. Eric O'Shaughnessy of Clean Kilowatts wrote it with Sushmita Jena and Dani Salyer. Voluntary power is what customers buy beyond what their utility must supply: green tariffs, purchase deals, and unbundled certificates. In 2023 about 9.7 million retail customers procured roughly 319 million megawatt-hours this way. Sales rose seventeen percent over 2022.

That volume equaled about forty-four percent of U.S. renewable sales excluding large hydro. It was about eight percent of all retail electricity. The series tracks buyers and sales back through 2013, splitting household enthusiasm from the corporate purchases that dominate volume. A new chapter follows energy storage entering voluntary products, and how offerings might adapt. For policymakers, the report is the scoreboard of demand that no mandate created.
doe-osti-2585480-sound-speeds-of-solids-:
Jack Borg and Dan Dolan of Sandia National Laboratories wrote report SAND2025-10120, printed in August 2025, on measuring sound speeds in solid materials. Their method uses an ultrasonic pulse receiver: a short sound pulse crosses a sample, and its travel time gives the speed of sound in that solid. Both compression waves and shear waves are covered.

Early chapters give background on the two wave types. A long middle chapter then guides the reader through taking measurements, step by step, as a lab handbook would. Analysis chapters explain the theory and a Matlab tool that finds the center of each received pulse. The report also covers density measurement with a balance kit, noting that a cylindrical sample 1.5 inches across fits the kit best and gives the strongest reading.
doe-osti-2586988-modeling-of-spin-squeez:
Eduardo Ibarra-Garcia-Padilla prepared this report, SAND2025-10500R, dated August 11, 2025, with Brandon Ruzic, Jonathan Bainbridge, and Peter Schwindt of Sandia National Laboratories. It models spin squeezing in optically pumped magnetometers, sensors that read magnetic fields with a hot atomic vapor. Squeezing is a quantum trick that cuts noise in one variable below the standard quantum limit.

The project goal is a magnetometer that beats that limit in field conditions, more than doubling usable bandwidth while holding world-class sensitivity. The theory work maps what limits sensitivity and bandwidth in terms of things an experimenter can set, such as cell temperature and probe laser detuning. It derives Cramer-Rao lower bounds, the floor on any measurement, under photon shot noise and spin projection noise. Squeezing is then folded into those bounds to predict the gains on offer.
doe-osti-2587585-biological-design-of-le:
Evan Ernst and Robert Martienssen of Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory wrote this final report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0018244, dated August 28, 2025. James Birchler and Eric Lam are among the teaming members, with partners at Brookhaven, Rutgers, and the University of Missouri. The project, which ran from September 2017 to March 2024, worked on the biological design of duckweeds for biodiesel.

Duckweeds, family Lemnaceae, are the world's smallest flowering plants, and they grow at a pace land crops cannot match. In good conditions they can double their fronds in 30 hours and yield 64 grams of biomass per gram of starting weight in a week, against 2.3 grams for corn. The team pursued genomic leads for raising lipid content, looked at dormant turions as end points for storing those oils, and analyzed the microbiomes that live with the plants. Open pond growth and easy harvest of dry material make duckweed a serious algae alternative.
doe-osti-2587617-parallel-runtime-interf:
Dan Bonachea, Katherine Rasmussen, Damian Rouson, and the Parallel Runtime Interface for Fortran Committee issued this specification, Revision 0.6, on September 16, 2025. It is Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report LBNL-2001698. The document defines PRIF, a standard link between Fortran compilers and the runtime libraries that power Fortran's built-in parallel features.

Modern Fortran lets a program split into images that run side by side and share data through coarrays. Under PRIF, the compiler turns those language features into calls, and a runtime library does the work. It allocates coarrays, syncs images, and runs atomic steps, events, teams, and joint routines. The split lets one compiler work with different runtime libraries and data links. The interface is written in standard Fortran syntax. It aims at portability across shared- and distributed-memory machines, operating systems, and processor types.
doe-osti-2588105-project-right-way-next-:
Scott Murphy is the named author of this Phase 1 performance report narrative for Project Right Way. The project is the Next Generation Melt Project of the American Cast Iron Pipe Company. It runs under award DE-CD0000084 from the Department of Energy's Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations. The office funds first-of-a-kind clean technology at working plants, under its industrial decarbonization program.

A melt project at an iron pipe works targets the furnace line, where metal is melted and most energy use and emissions concentrate. The narrative reports Phase 1 progress in the program's own terms. Its headline is steadiness. The project vision and objectives remain unchanged from the original plan. The execution approach has needed no significant adjustment, since current methods are proving effective. For a demonstration award, that on-plan report is itself the deliverable, setting up later construction and operating phases.
doe-osti-2588578-solar-energy-demonstrat:
Ken Kowalewitz, chairman of the South Hero Library Foundation board, and Keagan Calkins, library director, filed this final technical report for award DE-EE0010809. The project ran from October 2024 through March 2025. It was a solar energy demonstration at the Worthen Library in South Hero, Vermont. The library's five-year strategic plan, adopted in 2022, includes cutting reliance on fossil fuels.

Small projects run on borrowed expertise, and the report shows how. Two project planners were tapped from the community. One was a retired engineer who also sat on the Vermont Electric Cooperative board. The other was a town resident who had worked as an installer for a local solar company. Subtasks work through planning and legal review step by step, the way a tiny nonprofit executes a federal award. The demonstration framing means the array is also an exhibit. It shows a small island town what rooftop solar involves in practice.
doe-osti-2589922-detection-of-fissile-ma: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011866, by T. Classen, dated September 2025, is a short concept note on finding hidden fissile material with cosmic rays. A laboratory team at White Mountain Research Center found that primary cosmic rays striking heavy elements produce bursts of linked neutrons. In fissile material, those bursts can start fission chains and stamp a distinctive timing pattern. Geant4 simulations estimated signals and backgrounds at several distances and found unique, measurable signatures worth follow-up detector work.
doe-osti-2999071-arcade-analysis-methods:
Andrew Hahn, Adam Beauchaine, Titus Gray and co-workers at Sandia National Laboratories set out the analysis method and validation pathway for a tool named ARCADE, in report SAND2025-12807R, dated September 2025. ARCADE searches digital control system designs for the failure and attack paths an adversary would most likely use. Such full top-tier analysis has been out of reach for conventional tools.

A pilot run used Asherah, a published pressurised water reactor simulator whose data can be shared openly. The tool mapped every failure route in the plant model, then narrowed the view to routes that push fuel past safe temperatures. Some parts, such as the reactor coolant pumps, stood out as most safety-critical, while a turbine valve faded in importance. The report then formalises the search problem, tests how complete the hunt is, and lists what must still be built and proven before ARCADE is production ready.
doe-osti-3000482-the-three-dimensional-s:
Christopher Monahan of Colorado College wrote this final report for an Early Career award, DE-SC0023047, on the three-dimensional structure of the proton. Protons are not simple balls: quarks and the gluons that bind them swirl with momentum and spin. The project asked how gluons are spread in momentum, how quark and gluon motions correlate, and how computer calculations can guide experiments at the future Electron-Ion Collider.

Using lattice quantum chromodynamics, which simulates the strong force on a space-time grid, the team produced the first calculations of helicity parton distributions and generalised form factors through a pseudo-distribution method. Those quantities map both where the proton's parts sit and how they move. New tools for checking errors and new observables for testing lattice results came with them. Nine peer-reviewed papers, open software and trained early-career researchers round out the record.
doe-osti-3002157-an-overview-of-the-molt:
Ryan Chesser, Nicholas Termini, Shane Henderson, Difan Zhang, Vanda Glezakou, and Anthony Birri describe a data resource in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4159, dated September 2025. The resource is version 4.0 of the Molten Salt Thermal Properties Database, thermophysical part. Reactor designers use it to look up how molten salts behave at high heat: density, viscosity, surface tension, and heat conduction.

Version 4.0 adds surface tension data, with checked correlations for 294 chloride and fluoride salt mixes. The database now covers 976 distinct salt compositions. Entries were ranked by a quality method that weighs how much detail the source experiments report. The report also covers new prediction tools, including a thermal conductivity model checked against measured data. Salt-cooled and molten salt reactor teams are the main users.
doe-osti-3011738-enhanced-outcrop-methan:
Methane leaking from coal outcrops is captured in a pilot project closed out by Graham Stahnke of the Southern Ute Department of Energy under award DE-FE0032164. The final report, dated October 31, 2025, covers design, permitting, construction, and operation of pilot wells with a central delivery point on the Southern Ute Reservation in Colorado. Horizontal drilling reached into the coal seams.

Drilling plans show laterals run from a vertical well interception, with a vent well borehole designated EOMC-1 and measured depths near 4,380 feet. The project structure moves from pre drilling investigation through construction to operations. The report assembles the engineering record for the capture system.
doe-osti-3011864-residential-and-small-c:
Permitting, inspection, and interconnection timelines for small solar and storage projects are reviewed by Jesse Cruce, Dalila Lara, Noah Frey, Emily Dalecki, and Jeff Cook. The study updates a 2022 report and extends coverage from 2017 to 2023. Projects face approval by the local authority having jurisdiction and the electric utility before they can run.

Timelines vary widely across tens of thousands of jurisdictions and about 3,000 utilities. Results are weighted toward larger installers with higher volumes, so they may not match every jurisdiction. Phase timelines were worked out one by one and cannot simply be added into totals. California projects weigh heavily in the source data.
doe-osti-3014928-innovating-distributed-:
Lessons from the Innovating Distributed Embedded Energy Prize, called InDEEP, fill NLR/TP-5700-94984, dated January 2026, written by National Laboratory of the Rockies staff with two Sandia co-authors. The prize challenged teams to build distributed embedded energy conversion devices, a young field where energy is harvested inside structures and materials rather than by separate generators. Blake Boren led the author team.

The report argues the prize let participants attack engineering questions the field had barely touched: designing for emergent behavior, defining complete energy pathways, and setting robust test practices. It also credits the support structure around the contest. Flexible prize mechanics, sector scans, mentorship, webinars, and reviewer feedback lowered the barrier to entry and kept smaller teams competitive through the later rounds.
doe-osti-3020299-sample-preparation-labo:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-24-80022, by Stephanie Austad and nine co-authors, shares lessons from building the Sample Preparation Laboratory, a $100 to $200 million nuclear facility. Big nuclear projects have a history of cost overruns and delays under the traditional model, where a specially accredited firm manages everything. INL instead applied its own nuclear quality program over a commercial construction contractor.

The core of the approach is Commercial Grade Dedication, a method borrowed from operating plants. Engineers name the specific traits an item must have to do its safety job, then verify those traits by testing, inspection, or audits, without requiring suppliers to run full nuclear quality programs. The report calls this a first-of-a-kind use of dedication at this scale for a Hazard Category 3 facility. It details specifications, documentation, and supplier oversight so other projects can repeat the approach.
doe-osti-3020746-proposed-critical-think:
PNNL report by Michelle Dowling, Corey Fallon, and Eric Andersen, dated January 2026, proposes ways to measure critical thinking in people training to run the power grid. Grid operators reason under pressure, yet training programs rarely score the reasoning itself. The authors break critical thinking into testable techniques and define a metric for each, expressed as percentages of correct performance across training prompts.

For inductive reasoning, trainees see set examples and must draw the general conclusion; the metric is the share of correct conclusions. A matching metric covers deductive reasoning, where general statements are given and the right conclusions must follow. Other methods draw on direct experience and on what others pass along. Each metric can be computed for one exercise or a whole course, giving instructors a consistent yardstick for trainee judgment.
doe-osti-3020809-uncertainty-quantificat:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-26/8, by Zichao Wendy Di, Matthew J. Cherukara, and Tao Zhou, works on a gap in scientific imaging: a reconstructed image is only half an answer without knowing how wrong it might be. The report develops uncertainty quantification for inverse problems, the class of problems where measurements must be turned back into the object that produced them. Ptychography, an X-ray imaging method used at synchrotrons, serves as the test application.

The approach builds on maximum a posteriori estimation, where the best reconstruction balances fit to data against prior expectations. The authors show how the curvature of that objective at its minimum, captured by its Hessian matrix, approximates the covariance of the estimate. They handle the awkward cases too: singular curvature calls for a pseudo-inverse, and non-smooth priors need smoothing or generalized Hessians. A preprint version is dated February 21, 2026.
doe-osti-3366504-radiological-dose-conse:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-92283, ECAR-9159, by Bradley J. Schrader and dated May 2026, fixes the dose consequence modeling parameters Idaho's safety analysts must use. When a nuclear facility's safety case assumes an airborne release, the predicted public dose depends on atmospheric transport choices that could otherwise vary analyst by analyst. This engineering calculation standardizes them under DOE-STD-3009-2014 and NE-STD-1027-2025.

Receptor definitions anchor the method: a collocated worker at 100 meters and a maximally exposed member of the public at the site boundary point with the highest directional dose. The document also records the DOE-NRC memorandum context letting DOE analyses inform future NRC licensing of advanced reactors. Consistency, the ECAR argues, is what makes two safety cases comparable.
doe-osti-3367744-polk-carbon-storage-com:
Tampa Electric final report for DOE CarbonSAFE Phase 3 award DE-FE0032444, principal investigator Kristopher Stryker with Nathan Kirkconnell, assesses the Polk Carbon Storage Complex near the company's Florida power station. Phase 3 work characterizes a storage site before commercial commitment: geology, environmental review, and permitting groundwork. The report covers progress through the end of the performance period, which arrived earlier than planned.

An environmental information volume was in draft, bound for DOE's preliminary review in early 2026 had the project run to conclusion. The completed analysis found no environmental fatal flaws, permitting constraints, or significant adverse impacts for the site. The account is therefore a partial-phase record: characterization advanced, the final review loop did not. For a utility weighing carbon capture at an existing plant, even the unfinished homework is informative.
doe-osti-3375698-algae-hydrothermal-liqu:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory end-of-project report, by Peter J. Valdez and dated June 2026, closes the lab's algae hydrothermal liquefaction program. The method cooks wet algae in hot, pressurized water. Out comes a biocrude oil, much like a crude petroleum, with no need to dry the feed first. Drying is the step that sinks most algae fuel schemes on cost. The lab ran the process for years as its lead route from algae to fuel.

The closing report surveys the program's published work. One strand blended algae with forest product residue to stretch feed supply. A 2022 paper in Algal Research covers that mix. A second strand attacked ash, the grit that clogs the process. A hydrocyclone step strips ash from wastewater-grown algae before cooking. The lab also kept a rolling state of technology account, last set in a 2023 report, to track yields and costs year by year.
doe-osti-3377400-baseline-hypothetical-f:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-TR-2025-00687, dated September 30, 2025, designs a model plant that makes two medical isotopes by neutron activation. Nicholas Groden heads a five-author team. The work sits in the PRO-X program, under the Office of Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation. Molybdenum-99 and iodine-131 are workhorse isotopes for scans and therapy. Making them from activated targets, not fission, cuts proliferation risk. This baseline fixes the yardstick design for that route.

A 10-megawatt research reactor drives the plant. Tellurium dioxide feeds the iodine line; molybdenum trioxide feeds the molybdenum line. Output runs at 60 curies a week of iodine-131 and 5 curies a week of molybdenum-99. Three hot cells take in targets, extract, purify, and pack. A fourth handles waste. The whole site takes 763 square meters. The report then sets this design side by side with a fission-based twin to show where the routes diverge.
doe-osti-3377901-summary-of-gfl-inverter:
Haley Ross of the National Laboratory of the Rockies summarizes grid-forming inverter capability and performance requirements for Malawi in slides dated April 2026. The core of the deck is a comparison table for primary frequency response. It places Malawi's draft requirements beside IEEE 2800, the ESO, and EirGrid, row by row. The rows cover droop settings, a deadband of plus or minus 15 millihertz, reaction time, and settling time.

Site-specific figures appear for the Kanengo plant. They include a reaction time of 200 milliseconds, with full response expected within 15 seconds. Other slides state that reactive power has priority. Active power should be maintained during voltage drops. Below 85 percent voltage, the reduction in active power follows the battery design specifications. Modeling must include momentary cessation and protective trip features.
doe-osti-3409831-strong-solar-ready-vets:
Interstate Renewable Energy Council closes award DE-EE0010493 with a final report on Solar Ready Vets Network Phase 3. Pagan Poggione served as principal investigator. The project ran from October 1, 2023 to September 30, 2025. The program links military veterans with solar jobs.

Tables list real job titles and pay from partner employers. Roles shown include solar installer, electrical apprentice, and field service posts. Pay entries run from 17 dollars to 31.50 dollars per hour in the sample shown. Workforce groups can see which solar roles hire veterans and what those roles pay in practice. Job tables like these show the range of roles open to program graduates.
doe-osti-3424513-status-and-trends-in-th:
Eric O'Shaughnessy of Clean Kilowatts and Sushmita Jena of the National Laboratory of the Rockies report on the voluntary power market, with 2024 data. Their report, NLR/TP-6A20-98781, is dated August 2026. Voluntary buyers choose renewable power beyond what rules require.

Large business buyers anchor the market through long contracts. They sign power purchase deals or utility renewable contracts over many years. Small firms and households lack access to such bespoke deals. Past research credits big buyers with an outsized role in new renewable builds. Market watchers can see who drives green power growth.
doe-osti-3434801-automation-study-for-ai:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2023159, dated August 2026, studies automation for airworthiness and program protection software checks. John Sarracino, Matt Sottile, and P. Pirkelbauer lead the author list in the text. Certification of flight software is slow, hand-heavy work.

CodeQL earned praise as a strong middle path between rigid scanners and costly custom frameworks. Tests with AI tools found a clear flaw: the AI invented links between code elements. Safety case tools also proved immature and hard to use. The study maps where automation helps now and where human judgment must stay.
doe-osti-3484805-wind-turbine-materials-:
NLR/TP-5500-100353 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that covers a wind turbine materials recycling prize project. Ana Aday and John Kevern were the lab contacts. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-24-31305. Ground turbine blade waste goes into light cement mixes in this project.

Seven-day strength tests used three two-inch mortar cubes per mix. Strength tracked dry density closely across all mixes. Density thus serves as a handy strength predictor for these mixes. Blade waste that now fills landfills could instead lighten building materials with known strength.
doe-osti-3740108-characterization-of-sec:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4771, dated August 2026, maps the new compounds that form when glow tags are welded into aluminum. Six authors from Oak Ridge and Los Alamos are printed: Jordan Roach, Taylor Fetrow, Cheryl Hawk, Lindsay O'Brien, Tyler Spano, and Ashley Shields. Rare-earth oxide powders are stirred into welds so the joint glows under light, marking it as genuine. Welding heat can react those powders into fresh phases that shift the glow, so the team set out to name them.

Three tools did the naming: X-ray fluorescence maps, Raman spectra, and X-ray diffraction. Six taggants were tested, among them yttria, ceria, and oxides of praseodymium, dysprosium, and erbium. The yttria weld formed a second, rarer phase inside crater-like pits. Its spectrum closely matches a known garnet compound, which explains a colour shift seen in earlier work.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-ezekiel-da:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Minor Prophets pairs prophecy with Matthew's opening. Alexander Maclaren preached each piece as a sermon exposition. After the three named books, the volume adds St. Matthew chapters I to VIII. Short texts anchor every entry.

Ezekiel entries include Chambers of Imagery and The Dry Bones and the Spirit of Life. Daniel gives Youthful Confessors, Mene Tekel Peres, and Faith Stopping the Mouths of Lions. Hosea follows with The Valley of Achor and Israel Returning. Amos contributes The Sins of Society and Ripe for Gathering. The minor prophets proceed in book order from there. Maclaren turns dense prophecy into direct address for hearers.
four-famous-american-writers-washington-:
Cody tells the lives of Irving, Poe, Lowell, and Bayard Taylor for young American readers. The Irving chapters run from a first voyage up the Hudson to Rip Van Winkle and The Alhambra's success. Poe's story includes how The Raven was written and his years of living by literature.

The Lowell section opens at Elmwood, the family home west of Cambridge near Mount Auburn cemetery. James Russell Lowell was born there on February 22, 1819, behind a high green hedge of pines and willows. Sherwin Cody published the four biographies in 1899. Each life is broken into short, clear chapters for school-age readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAWilsonEdwinP:
Philip Taubman and Jeff Gerth reported for the New York Times, in an article dated October 12, on two former CIA men in a new business. Edwin P. Wilson and Frank E. Terpil had joined a California electronics company to market sensitive American technology abroad.

Wilson and Terpil became the most notorious ex-agents of their generation, accused of selling arms, explosives, and training to Libya's Muammar Gaddafi. Articles like this one caught them at the start of that exposure, still presenting themselves as legitimate exporters. The piece is preserved as early reporting on the Wilson-Terpil enterprise, before the trials made them famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EdelmanRichardP: Nsia-EdelmanRichardP Edelman Richard P: the made public government document, captured as titled, subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued, an obscure item, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-the-plays-of-christo: The Plays of Christopher Marlowe: the title page - the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single page, dated material, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the literature and readers.
history-of-the-girondists-volume-i-perso:
Alphonse de Lamartine wrote this history of the Girondists, the moderate patriots of the French Revolution. H T Ryde translated it for a London edition of 1856. The set runs to three volumes, and a portrait of Robespierre fronts this first. Lamartine calls the work personal memoirs drawn from unpublished sources.

His advertisement skips the Revolution's earlier epochs without apology. The tale starts with the men, not the annals. Lamartine judges the settlement of 1791 with a poet's sweep. He finds its flaw not in one point but in its whole frame. Readers get history as portrait gallery, warm, partisan, and vivid.
illustrated-catalogue-of-the-collections:
James Stevenson compiled this catalogue of goods from the Pueblos of Zuni in New Mexico and Wolpi in Arizona in 1881. It appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology report printed in Washington in 1884. The finds come from two Pueblo towns with strong craft traditions.

Entries name bowls and other clay ware one by one. Native names for each piece are given beside the English note. Morning star and god star figures on bowls are recorded. Small yellow water bowls and deer designs also appear. The list helps readers see range in form, color, and design.
nasa-tm-19640004350-a-4-kilowatt-steam-r:
Roy L. Johnsen of Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1963 interagency meeting. It studies a small solar power system for space use. Sunlight heats a boiler, and steam spins a turbine for power. Engineers call that layout a steam Rankine cycle system.

An earlier study had found steam compared well with mercury as the working fluid. That work treated a much larger fifty-kilowatt system. Johnsen scaled the question down to about four kilowatts of output. He reused parts and weights from the Sunflower I solar unit. The aim was to spot any big effects of choosing steam at small size.
nasa-tm-19660001379-experimental-x-ray-s:
James H Wharton and William L Prince at Marshall developed X-ray methods for finding hidden stress in aluminum alloys for this September 13, 1965, report. The alloys are precipitation hardened, strengthened by tiny particles formed inside the metal. X-ray diffraction can reveal stress without cutting the part open. The authors developed the techniques and then evaluated how well they worked.

Hidden stress can warp a part or start a crack later. Measuring it before flight is a quality safeguard. Aluminum alloys formed much of a rocket's structure at the time. A reliable X-ray method let inspectors check finished parts, rather than trusting the process alone. The materials studied are named in the report.
nasa-tm-19660012976-effects-of-adrenalin:
R Coler, William A McLaurin, and Donald R Young at Ames tested what two common drugs do to a person's work. Adrenalin and insulin were given to human subjects after about eight hours of enforced work or rest. Each drug group had nine subjects, and each person served in both the working and the resting state on separate occasions. Memory, reaction speed, and steadiness were measured.

After injection, performance fell on all three tests, for all subjects. That drop appeared in workers and in resting subjects alike. Ten test sessions ran before injection and seven after it. For flight medicine, the message was clear: drug effects on a tired crew cannot be guessed from a rested one.
nasa-tm-19680017402-thermal-degradation-:
Robert A. Jewell of Langley Research Center studied how Pyrrone films break down under heat in this NASA report. Pyrrones are ladder-type polymers built to survive extreme temperatures. Jewell heated several films in air and in vacuum across a very wide temperature range.

Thermogravimetric analysis tracked weight loss during steady and programmed heating. In hard vacuum, average losses reached about thirty percent at the top test temperatures reported. Mass spectrometry showed carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and water as the main gases given off. The films also soaked up five to seven percent of their weight in water from room air. That uptake, plus sample history and shape, strongly affected test results.
nasa-tm-19680019652-explorer-35-measurem:
G. P. Serbu, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this 1968 preprint, X-615-68-232. He reports early observations of low energy plasma, the thin charged gas around the Moon, gathered by the Explorer 35 spacecraft in lunar orbit. Explorer 35 entered its Moon orbit on July 22, 1967, circling once every eleven and a half hours.

A flat multi-grid sensor aboard the craft worked as a retarding potential analyzer, sorting charged particles by energy. By sweeping its voltage, the sensor measured currents from both electrons and ions below five hundred electron volts. Serbu presents these first spectra as a preliminary look at the plasma environment a lunar orbiter actually meets.
nasa-tm-19710018469-creep-fatigue-analys:
S S Manson, G R Halford, and M H Hirschberg of the Lewis Research Center set out a new way to predict hot metal failure in this paper. It was prepared for a May 1971 meeting in San Francisco. Their method is called strain range partitioning. It treats creep fatigue, the damage done when hot parts flex again and again under load.

The key idea splits each strain cycle by its cause. Some strain is quick plastic flow, some is slow creep, in either direction. Each part is tied to service life by its own equation. A simple rule then adds the damage shares until failure. Test results covered a chromium molybdenum steel, with early data on stainless steel.
operation-r-s-v-p:
H. Beam Piper built his short story Operation R.S.V.P., first printed in Amazing Stories in January 1951, entirely out of diplomatic letters. The year inside the fiction is 1984, and two rival world blocs, the Union of East European Soviet Republics and the United Peoples' Republics of East Asia, are corresponding with lethal politeness.

The opening letter helpfully announces a successful test of a nuclear-rocket missile named Marxist Victory. Its writer helpfully adds that the missile's range exceeds, by half again, the distance to the other side's capital, Nanking, and hopes a river dispute might now be reconsidered. Piper's joke is the form itself: courteous foreign-ministry language carrying an unmistakable threat, answered in kind as the exchange of notes escalates.
palestine-or-the-holy-land-from-the-earl:
The Reverend Michael Russell wrote Palestine, or the Holy Land, as a history from the earliest period to his own time. His preface explains the book's design. Earlier volumes, he says, chose one of two plans. Some gave bare annals of the Jewish people. Others gave topographical descriptions of the land alone. Russell unites the two plans in one volume.

His chapters join narrative to place. The constitution, antiquities, religion, and literature of the Hebrews appear. Their statistics appear too. He traces the Twelve Tribes settling on the Jordan's banks. Shepherds gradually become agriculturalists there. Power concentrates into one man's hands. A chapter on Hebrew literature and religion follows the same ground. Russell wrote for the general reader, and his preface promises nothing left unexplored.
physics-and-politics-or-thoughts-on-the-:
Walter Bagehot's Physics and Politics applies the principles of natural selection and inheritance to political society. The first chapter, The Preliminary Age, opens on the sudden acquisition of physical knowledge in his century: railways, telegraphs, and a new world of ideas in the air. By it, he says, everything is made an antiquity, since science reads every bit of earth as a record of causes.

The contents promise the use of conflict, two chapters on nation-making, the age of discussion, and verifiable progress politically considered. Bagehot asks how nations form durable habits, and why discussion can only govern after conflict has done its work.
saltbush-bill-j-p: A. B. Paterson, Andrew Barton Banjo Paterson, whose life dates are given as 1864 to 1941, wrote Saltbush Bill, J.P., and Other Verses. Paterson is named as author of The Man from Snowy River, Rio Grande, and An Outback Marriage. A publisher's note says Major Paterson had been on active service in Egypt for the past eighteen months. Only a few pieces in the volume, the publishers state, were seen by him in proof, and he is not responsible for the selection, arrangement, or title.
sir-joshua-reynolds-a-collection-of-fift:
Estelle M. Hurll gathered fifteen pictures by Sir Joshua Reynolds in this Masterpieces of Art volume, issued by Houghton Mifflin under a 1900 copyright. A self-portrait of Reynolds fronts the set. Hurll adds an opening essay, notes on books of reference, and readings of each picture.

A directory traces each painting's history, and an outline table marks the chief events of Reynolds's life. Hurll writes for students and art lovers who cannot reach the great galleries. Her readings teach how to look: at pose, color, and character in the work of Britain's leading portrait painter of the eighteenth century.
the-art-of-perfumery-and-methods-of-obta:
G. W. Septimus Piesse wrote The Odors of Flowers. Here his full title promises to teach how plant scents are got. It also teaches how to make perfumes for the handkerchief. Scented powders, scented vinegars, tooth pastes, pomatums, cosmetics, and perfumed soap are all covered. An added part treats the colors of flowers and made-up fruit essences.

An opening picture shows a drying house for herbs. Bunches of the grower's herbs hang from the roof rafters. Warm cupboards, heated by a flue from a fire below, hold long canvas trays of flower buds and rose leaves until they dry. Piesse begins his craft at that plain first step: saving the scent before it fades.
the-mystery-of-murray-davenport-a-story-:
Robert Neilson Stephens's The Mystery of Murray Davenport is dated 1903. Its subtitle reads A Story of New York at the Present Day. Only a list of the author's works and a partial contents are present here, so the story does not appear. Stephens's earlier historical romances head the list: An Enemy to the King, The Continental Dragoon, and The Road to Paris, among six titles.

A frontispiece caption asks, Do you know what a Jonah is? Contents shown run to nine chapters. Mr. Larcher Goes Out in the Rain opens the book, followed by One Out of Suits with Fortune and A Ready-Money Man. An Unprofitable Child, A Lodging by the River, and Mystery Begins carry the visible list.
the-origin-of-species-by-means-of-natura: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species appears here in the sixth London edition, with all additions and corrections. A prefatory list notes three editions: the first of 1859, the second of 1860, and the sixth of 1872, called the definitive edition. Only the title page, quotations from Whewell, Butler, and Bacon, and the heading of Darwin's historical sketch are present here, so the argument itself does not appear. The subtitle promises the preservation of favoured races in the struggle for life.
the-poet-s-poet-essays-on-the-character-:
Elizabeth Atkins's The Poet's Poet collects essays on the character and mission of the poet, as a century and a half of English verse has interpreted them. Atkins, an instructor in English at the University of Minnesota, dedicates the volume to Hartley and Nelly Alexander. Her preface complains that poets' own statements about their calling have received less attention than they deserve.

Critics, she notes, tend to assume that a poet, like a criminal, is the worst judge of his own case. Atkins doubts that view, since Plato's famous challenge was aimed at Poetry herself. Her method is a review of the whole body of such verse. She does not closely analyse single long poems like Wordsworth's Prelude or Browning's Sordello. She promises impartial treatment of every side. Beneath the contradictions, she expects to find an essential unity in how poets view themselves.
the-reign-of-andrew-jackson-a-chronicle-:
Frederic Austin Ogg traces Jackson's career in a textbook edition copyrighted by Yale University Press in 1919, as volume twenty of the Chronicles of America. Chapter one begins with Andrew Jackson the elder, a Scotch-Irish Presbyterian tenant farmer from near Carrickfergus who crossed to the Western World after the peace of 1763.

Eleven chapters follow the Creek War, New Orleans, Florida, the death of King Caucus, the Webster-Hayne debate, nullification, the bank war, Indian removal, and the Jacksonian succession. Students get a compact frontier-centered account of how Jacksonian democracy formed and governed.
the-uncollected-writings-of-thomas-de-qu:
James Hogg edited the first volume of Thomas De Quincey's uncollected writings, published in London by Swan Sonnenschein in 1890. The set runs to two volumes, with Hogg supplying a preface and annotations. He calls the gathering the last fruit off an old tree, borrowing a phrase from Walter Savage Landor.

Hogg knew De Quincey closely from about 1850 until the author's death in 1859. During those years he helped prepare the Selections Grave and Gay for the press. His preface therefore speaks from personal acquaintance, not distant scholarship. Readers get periodical pieces rescued from obscurity, introduced by a friend who worked beside their author.
united-states-congress-senate-committee-: Amnesty and Pardon for Political Prisoners, U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary. The amnesty plea. This book preserves that report. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
watch-and-clock-escapements-a-complete-s: Watch and Clock Escapements offers a complete study in theory and practice. Compilers drew it from the well-known escapement serials in The Keystone. That journal published it at Philadelphia in 1904, with nearly two hundred original illustrations. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only, so the lessons themselves are not shown. Contents promise three chapters. The detached lever escapement comes first. The cylinder escapement and the chronometer escapement follow. A brief account of how the escapement arose goes with them.
what-i-saw-in-california-a-description-o:
Edwin Bryant, once alcalde of San Francisco, wrote What I Saw in California in 1849. The book describes the land, its weather, its products, and its gold mines. It also gives routes and fresh news for people who plan to move west. An added part holds state papers and letters that back the gold reports, with tests of the gold's true worth.

Chapter one sketches the map of Upper California, from Oregon down to Sonora and Lower California. Bryant notes old rule, forts, missions, ports, and trade. The San Joaquin valley and river enter the account early. Readers get a guide made at the height of the gold rush.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: Only the Project Gutenberg header is shown for this Widger set, so the quotations do not appear. The source is Albert Bigelow Paine's writings on Mark Twain. David Widger's set is number 11 in his Quotations series. The header gives a release date of January 2003 and etext number 3643. First posting is dated July 1, 2001, and the edition is number 10. The rest repeats the standard Gutenberg header text on law, donations, and the archive foundation.
